title: CAR-T cells for children with CNS tumours
official: CARTUNE: Phase I study of repeated intracerebroventricular administration of B7H3 targeting CAR-T cells in children and young adults with recurrent/refractory high grade CNS tumours
summary:
Background and study aims
Central nervous system (CNS) tumours are abnormal growths of cells in the brain or spinal cord. Treatment options include neurosurgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, which work well for some patients. However, other patients either don’t respond to available treatments or the disease returns, and there are no effective options in these cases.
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are blood cells genetically engineered to recognise and kill tumour cells. Lasting responses have been achieved in leukaemia, and CAR T products have been approved for use as part of standard treatment for some blood cancers. Early clinical trial data indicate the CAR T cells may also work in non-blood cancers. Currently there are no CAR T cells approved for CNS tumours. We have developed CAR T cells that recognise a target called B7H3 on CNS tumour cells. This study aims to test whether giving these CAR T cells to patients with CNS tumours is safe and what dose to use.

Who can participate?
Patients with relapsed or refractory high-grade CNS tumour, aged 1-18 years (UK) or 1-24 years (Netherlands)

What does the study involve?
We will collect T cells from the participants’ blood to make the CAR T cells in a specialized laboratory. We will put a new gene into the T cells so they can recognise the B7H3 target and attack the tumour. If not already present, participants will have a device called the Ommaya Reservoir surgically placed under the skin of their scalp. This device will be used to administer the CAR T cells into the fluid around the brain and to monitor and treat the pressure inside the skull. Within 7 days before the CAR T cell infusion, participants will have tests to confirm they are still eligible for the infusion. If so, participants will receive the first CAR T cell infusion and will remain in hospital for at least 2 weeks for monitoring. If there are no safety concerns, participants may have up to 5 additional CAR T cell infusions approximately 1 month apart from each other. After each infusion, patients will be monitored for safety, with tests including MRI scans, blood tests and measurement of the pressure inside the brain.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Leukapheresis is required to collect participants’ T cells (a type of white blood cell) from the blood for the manufacture of CAR T cells. The T cells are collected using a catheter inserted into a large vein. Pain, bruising and a small amount of bleeding can occur around the insertion site. Pain medication and application of a pressure dressing will be used if needed. The small risk of fainting will be prevented by having the participant sit or lie down during the procedure. The anticoagulant used during the cell collection procedure can reduce the calcium levels in the blood. This can cause tingling/numbness or muscle cramps. This will be prevented by giving calcium supplements if needed.
It is expected that most participants will already have an Ommaya reservoir (or similar catheter) in place at the time of trial registration. An Ommaya reservoir is a catheter placed in one of the fluid-filled spaces in the brain (ventricle) attached to a reservoir implanted under the scalp. If not already present, participants will have an Ommaya reservoir (or similar catheter) inserted by an experienced neurosurgeon prior to the CAR T-cell infusion to allow the delivery of CAR T cells directly into the ventricles of the brain (intracerebroventricular infusion) and the monitoring and, if necessary, treatment of raised intracranial pressure (ICP). This procedure may be combined with a tumour biopsy to confirm eligibility for the trial and/or tumour debulking when clinically indicated.
Insertion of the Ommaya is a surgical procedure performed while the participant is under general anaesthesia. The risk of serious complication due to implanting this device is <2%. Complications include infection, bleeding or swelling in the brain causing loss of function, such as weakness, pain, numbness, speech, swallowing or visual problems; difficulties with memory and cognition; and epilepsy. This is usually temporary and mild but can be serious and sustained in rare cases. Antibiotics will be given to prevent infection. Post-procedure observation is at least 6 hours, and supportive care will be provided as required if a complication occurs. 
The CAR T-cell infusion via the Ommaya reservoir will be performed by a practitioner trained in the administration of medications via this device. Participants will be closely monitored for 6 hours after each infusion. 
After the first CAR T-cell infusion, participants will be monitored in hospital for at least 14 days with daily assessments, including neurological examination, with increased frequency as clinically indicated.
Once participants complete 28 days post the first CAR T-cell infusion, they will be assessed for eligibility for additional CAR T-cell infusions. Participants may receive up to 6 CAR T infusions in total, approximately 1 month apart from each other. For the second and subsequent infusions, participants will remain as inpatients for at least 7 days for monitoring. During the first 14 days after each infusion, participants should reside within 1-2 hours' travel from a suitably equipped children’s hospital with expertise in the management of brain tumour patients, including neurosurgery. 
Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is characterised by fever, hypotension, and, in severe cases, hypoxia and/or other organ dysfunction (liver, renal, cardiac). Severe CRS requires high-dependency supportive care and is usually self-limiting but may be fatal. Participants developing CRS will receive supportive care, including intravenous fluids, supplementary oxygen and, if needed, ventilatory/inotropic support on the intensive care unit. Treatment with tocilizumab is highly effective. Other agents are available for management of CRS that is unresponsive to tocilizumab.
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a type of neurotoxicity which can occur in participants after receiving CAR T cells. It is of variable severity, mild and reversible in most cases. Severe cases present with aphasia, obtundation, delirium and seizures. In rare cases fatalities have been reported. Participants will receive supportive treatment with anticonvulsants and corticosteroids and, if required, intensive care including sedation and ventilation.
Neurotoxicity can occur due to activation of CAR T cells and associated swelling at the tumour site when the tumour is located in the brain or spine (tumour inflammation associated neurotoxicity or TIAN). TIAN can result in transient worsening of pre-existing neurological symptoms (e.g., cranial nerve deficits or ataxia in brainstem tumours; or back pain in spinal cord tumours). In severe cases, TIAN can cause raised ICP, resulting in headache and vomiting, or impending herniation syndromes, which are life-threatening and need urgent intervention. Participants with spinal cord tumours may develop urinary retention or reduced power or sensation in extremities.

Where is the study run from?
Cancer Research UK and University College London Cancer Trials Centre (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
June 2026 to December 2035

Who is funding the study?
Medical Research Council (UK)

Who is the main contact?
CARTUNE Trial Manager, ctc.CARTUNE@ucl.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age:
1.1. UK: ≥1 and ≤18 years
1.2. Netherlands: ≥1 and ≤24 years
2. Evidence of relapsed or refractory high-grade CNS tumour
3. Exhaustion of standard of care options with curative intent
4. Expression of B7H3 protein in biopsy/resection material obtained either in primary or relapse/refractory setting, measured by immunohistochemistry (IHC), H-score ≥100
5. Radiographically evaluable disease
6. Negative pregnancy test (if applicable) 
7. Agreement to use adequate contraception (if applicable)
8. Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion criteria for trial registration:
1. Bulky disease at time of CAR-T cell infusion
2. Diffuse midline glioma (DMG)
3. Pre-existing significant neurological disorder (other than CNS tumour-related)
4. Clinically significant systemic illness or medical condition (e.g., significant cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic or other organ dysfunction), that in the judgement of the investigator, is likely to interfere with assessment of safety or efficacy of the investigational regimen and its requirements
5. Primary immunodeficiency or history of autoimmune disease (e.g., Crohn’s, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) requiring systemic immunosuppression / systemic disease-modifying agents within the last 2 years
6. Any contraindication to Ommaya reservoir (or similar catheter) insertion
7. Inability to tolerate leukapheresis
8. Performance status: Karnofsky (age ≥10 years) or Lansky (age <10) score <50%  
9. Life expectancy <3 months
10. Oxygen saturation ≤90% in air
11.	Active hepatitis B, C or HIV infection
12.	Uncontrolled fungal, bacterial, viral or other infection
13.	Absolute neutrophil count ≤1.0 x 10e9/L, platelets ≤50 x 10e9/L, lymphocytes ≤0.25 x 10e9/L
14. Total bilirubin ≥1.5 x ULN
15.	AST or ALT ≥3 x ULN 
16. Serum creatinine ≥1.5 X ULN for age. If serum creatinine ≥1.5 x ULN, the potential participant can be included if creatinine clearance is >60 ml/min/1.73 m² (as per local practice) 
17.	Coagulation tests (PT and aPTT) outside the local reference ranges (correction with blood products to achieve normal range is permitted)
18.	Post-pubertal subjects who are pregnant or breastfeeding
19. Known allergy to DMSO (or any component of the ATIMP)
20. Systemic corticosteroid therapy ≥0.05 mg/kg dexamethasone daily (or equivalent) at time of CAR-T cell infusion. Corticosteroid physiologic replacement therapy is allowed. 

Exclusion criteria for first TE9-28z-iTAG2 CAR-T infusion:
1. Bulky disease at time of TE9-28z-iTAG2 CAR-T cell infusion
2. Performance status: Karnofsky (age ≥10 years) or Lansky (age <10 years) score <50%  
3. Uncontrolled fungal, bacterial, viral or other infection
4. Absolute neutrophil count ≤1.0 x 10e9/L, platelets ≤50 x 10e9/L, lymphocytes ≤0.25 x 10e9/L
5. Coagulation tests (PT and aPTT) outside the local reference ranges (correction with blood products to achieve normal range is permitted)
6. Absence of functional Ommaya Reservoir (or similar catheter) in situ.
7. Absence of baseline imaging of tumour performed prior to first CAR-T cell infusion 
8. Systemic corticosteroid therapy ≥0.05 mg/kg dexamethasone daily (or equivalent) at time of CAR-T cell infusion. Corticosteroid physiologic replacement therapy is allowed. 
9. Less than 2 weeks following completion of standard-of-care radiotherapy or systemic anti-cancer treatment.
10. Less than 3 weeks or 5 half-lives, whichever is shorter, after treatment with agents in any other early-phase clinical trial. 

Exclusion criteria for subsequent CAR-T cell infusions:
1. Occurrence of dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) with prior TE9-28z-iTAG2 CAR-T cell infusions. In patients in dose levels 2 or 3 who experience a DLT, subsequent CAR-T infusions may be given at the next lowest dose level if the patient has fully recovered from the toxicity.
2. Uncontrolled fungal, bacterial, viral or other infection
3. Imaging evidence of progressive disease following previous TE9-28z-iTAG2 CAR-T infusion
4. Systemic corticosteroid therapy ≥0.05 mg/kg dexamethasone daily (or equivalent) at time of CAR-T cell infusion. Corticosteroid physiologic replacement therapy is allowed.
